messages.author: 746e3448cb1cf6e5
messages.subject: What is A[1] and why is it -nan?
parts:
I'm aware that I'm not supposed to post here if the 'count' number is small, but I am getting a lot of these "exceptions" and I'd like to understand what they are and how to avoid them. Here is what the exception says:

The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times after warmup on chain 2
 count
Exception thrown at line 54: multiply: A[1] is -nan, but must not be nan! 1
When a numerical problem occurs, the Hamiltonian proposal gets rejected.
See http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#exception-hamiltonian-proposal-rejected
If the number in the 'count' column is small, do not ask about this message on stan-users.

A[1] is not part of my code; this is something that Stan must create internally (though I'm not sure what it's referring to). Here is my Stan code:

data {
  int N; //current number of subjects
  int P; //number of non-treatment covariates
  int J; //number of treatments
  matrix[N, P] X; //covariate values
  matrix[N, J] T; //treatments
  int Y[4, N]; //attendence outcomes
  row_vector[4] zeroToThree; // just the numbers 0, 1, 2, and 3
}
transformed data {
  matrix[N, 4] Ym1;
  
  for (n in 1:N) Ym1[n, 1] = 0;
  for (week in 2:4) for (n in 1:N) Ym1[n, week] = 1 - Y[week - 1, n];
}
parameters {
  real alpha; //overall intercept
  vector[P] beta;  //vector of coefficients for X
  vector[J] theta_raw;  //vector of coefficients for T
  real delta; //linear effect of week
  vector[N] b_raw; //couple-specific intercepts
  
  real<lower=0> tau;
  real<lower=0> sigma_theta;
  real mu_theta;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[J] theta;
  vector[N] b;
    
  // matt trick
  theta = theta_raw * sigma_theta + mu_theta;
  b = b_raw * tau;
}
model {
  matrix[N, 4] eta;
  
  //priors
  alpha ~ normal(0, 10);
  beta ~ normal(0, 10);
  delta ~ normal(0, 10);
  b_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  theta_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
  mu_theta ~ normal(0, 1);
  sigma_theta ~ normal(0, 1);
  tau ~ normal(0, 1);
  //model
  eta = alpha + (b + X * beta + T * theta) * rep_row_vector(1, 4) +
        rep_vector(1, N) * zeroToThree * delta;
  for (j in 1:4) Y[j] ~ bernoulli_logit(col(eta, j));
}

Line 54, where the exception occurs, is the line in the model section where eta is assigned. Any pointers on what this could refer to would be appreciated.

messages.subject: Re: What is A[1] and why is it -nan?
parts: What would cause either beta or theta to go to NaN? My first thought, after reading that real parameters are initialized to NaN before they are first defined, was that I was using them before they were set to something that wasn't NaN. But I have priors for everything, and that doesn't seem to be what's happening here. What would cause the parameters to go to NaN, with them having relatively simple normal priors (theta uses a "Matt trick")? It's notable that it says they are NaN, not Inf.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: What is A[1] and why is it -nan?
parts:
What can happen is that a value goes off to infinity due to
improper posteriors or bad numerical problems, then you get
an infinite gradient and multiplication gives you NaN.

You can track down what's going wrong with print().

You can also reduce adapt_delta if it only happens occasionally
and that might solve the problem by making the Hamiltonian
simulation more accurate (if the problem is numerical rather
than an improper posterior).

- Bob
